questions.q: What two things does a primary key guarantee?
options: Every value is sorted alphabetically
The table can have no foreign keys
Every value is unique, and no value is ever NULL
The column must be an INT data type
questions.explain: Uniqueness plus NOT NULL together mean a primary key value always identifies exactly one row.

questions.q: What is a composite primary key?
options: A primary key made of two or more columns together, where the combination is unique even though no single column is
A key that spans multiple databases
A primary key that changes value over time
A primary key with no data type
questions.explain: AdventureWorks2012's SalesOrderDetail is keyed on SalesOrderID plus SalesOrderDetailID together, not either column alone.

questions.q: By default, what kind of index does creating a primary key build?
options: A clustered index, unless you explicitly specify NONCLUSTERED
No index at all
A filtered index
A nonclustered index, unless you explicitly specify CLUSTERED
questions.explain: Ties back to Lesson 88 — a primary key defaults to clustered, physically sorting the table by that key.

questions.q: Why name a primary key constraint explicitly, like PK_Department?
options: SQL Server requires an explicit name or the CREATE TABLE fails
It makes the column NOT NULL automatically
It gives you a predictable name to reference later if you need to drop or alter it
It's required for composite keys only
questions.explain: Without an explicit name, SQL Server auto-generates one that's harder to predict and reference in future scripts.

questions.q: How do you add a primary key to a table that already exists?
options: DROP TABLE and recreate it with the same name
ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY (...)
UPDATE the table's schema property directly
You cannot add a primary key after CREATE TABLE
questions.explain: ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT is the standard way to add a primary key to an existing table.
